Microsoft Kiota APIPlugin manifest generation from OpenAPI spec (CVE-2026-59864) AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts execution of `kiota plugin add` / `kiota plugin generate -t APIPlugin`, the propagation point where an attacker-controlled OpenAPI description's x-ai-adaptive-card / x-ai-capabilities extensions are written verbatim into `<name>-apiplugin.json`. Surfaces the OpenAPI source and kiota version so analysts can confirm whether a poisoned static_template.file path (../ or absolute) was minted. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact CLI verbs (`plugin add`/`plugin generate`) plus the `APIPlugin` template type and the `kiota` binary (confirmed on the self-contained linux-x64 1.32.4 release; also runs as kiota.exe / `dotnet kiota` on Windows dev hosts). This is the one host-observable event in the chain — where the poisoned static_template.file is emitted. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4jwf-m4wg-8p66 • https://github.com/microsoft/kiota/pull/7892
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately generating M365 Copilot/Teams plugins from trusted internal OpenAPI specs
  • CI/CD pipeline auto-regenerating plugin manifests on each build
  • Engineer following Kiota plugin tutorials/PoC testing
  • Platform team standardising internal API plugins from a vetted spec registry
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the command line's OpenAPI source (`-d`/`--openapi`) — is it a remote URL or third-party/untrusted spec? Confirm the kiota version; 1.32.4 and below are vulnerable, 1.32.5+ is patched. 2) Contain: quarantine the generated `<name>-apiplugin.json`, block its packaging/sideload to Copilot/Teams, and upgrade kiota to 1.32.5+ then regenerate. 3) Hunt: grep all generated manifests for `response_semantics.static_template.file` values containing `../`, absolute paths, UNC (`\\`), Windows drive (`C:\`), or `file://`/`http` URIs; find other plugins built from the same spec source.

| where ProcessCommandLine has "plugin"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "APIPlugin"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "plugin"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "APIPlugin"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

Kiota-generated *-apiplugin.json manifest written to disk (CVE-2026-59864 artifact) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces the write of a `<name>-apiplugin.json` Copilot/Teams plugin manifest by kiota so analysts can open it and inspect the `response_semantics.static_template.file` field for a path/URL-injected traversal (../, absolute, UNC, drive, or file/http URI). This is the exact artifact that carries the CWE-22/CWE-829 payload before it is sideloaded downstream. Rationale: Uses Kiota's fixed output naming convention `<name>-apiplugin.json` (per the advisory) scoped to a kiota/dotnet writer. It hands the analyst the precise file to open and check for a `..`/absolute/UNC/URI static_template.file value — the injected payload — which endpoint file telemetry cannot content-match directly. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4jwf-m4wg-8p66 • https://github.com/microsoft/kiota/pull/7892
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Copilot/Teams plugin builds writing a benign relative static_template.file
  • CI runners regenerating manifests on every commit
  • Developer testing plugin generation locally
  • Repo tooling re-emitting manifests during dependency bumps
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the flagged `-apiplugin.json` and read `functions[].capabilities.response_semantics.static_template.file` — flag if it contains `../`, a leading `/`, `\\`, `C:\`, or a `file://`/`http` URI (patched kiota 1.32.5+ rejects these). 2) Contain: block the manifest from being packaged/sideloaded to Copilot/Teams and upgrade kiota to 1.32.5+, then regenerate from a trusted spec. 3) Hunt: enumerate other `-apiplugin.json` files across build hosts and source repos produced from the same OpenAPI source and re-scan their static_template.file values.

| where FileName endswith "-apiplugin.json"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("kiota","kiota.exe","dotnet","dotnet.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "kiota"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| where ActingProcessName has "kiota" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "kiota"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Better-Auth SCIM global user deletion via /scim/v2/Users from unsanctioned caller AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts DELETE requests to the better-auth SCIM Users endpoint (/scim/v2/Users/:id) coming from a source IP that has never previously driven SCIM traffic. On affected @better-auth/scim (>=1.4.0-beta.27 <=1.6.21, 1.7.0-beta.0-9) a low-privileged authenticated user can mint a SCIM token with a colliding provider ID and DELETE the global Better Auth user plus sessions. Legitimate SCIM deprovisioning originates from the IdP's fixed egress; a delete from a fresh caller IP is the collision-abuse signal. Rationale: Uses the exact endpoint string from the advisory (DELETE /scim/v2/Users/:id — the highest-impact non-org deletion path) and the baseline anti-join on caller IP to separate colliding-token abuse from legitimate IdP deprovisioning, which always comes from a fixed egress. No endpoint/EDR telemetry exists for an inbound HTTP authz flaw, so only web-log platforms are populated. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/scim/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/scim
ATT&CKT1531 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IdP (Entra/Okta) deprovisioning from a newly rotated egress IP not seen in the 30d baseline
  • IdP failover to a secondary datacenter with a different public IP
  • Scheduled SCIM connector migrated to a new host/IP
  • Authorized penetration test or SCIM integration testing against the endpoint
  • Admin manually calling the SCIM API from a jump host during troubleshooting
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the DELETE events; identify the caller IP, csUserName, User-Agent and the /Users/:id targets; confirm the IP is NOT your sanctioned IdP egress and decode the SCIM bearer token's provider ID to see if it collides with an SSO/OIDC/OAuth/social provider namespace. 2) Contain: Revoke the offending SCIM token, disable SCIM token generation (canGenerateToken) for non-privileged users, block the source IP, and restore deleted users/sessions from backup. 3) Hunt: Audit scimProvider rows for providerId values matching other account providers, review PUT/PATCH activity on the same endpoint from the same caller, and upgrade to @better-auth/scim 1.6.22 or 1.7.0-beta.10.
// Baseline = IPs that legitimately drove SCIM in the prior 30d (your IdP egress)
let SanctionedScimCallers = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where csUriStem has "/scim/v2/Users"
    | summarize by cIP;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csUriStem has "/scim/v2/Users"
| where csMethod == "DELETE"
| where scStatus in (200, 204)            // successful global-user deletion
| join kind=leftanti SanctionedScimCallers on cIP   // delete from an IP never before seen issuing SCIM
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csUserName, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName, Computer, sPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Better-Auth SCIM profile/email rewrite fan-out across many /scim/v2/Users resources AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single caller issuing PUT/PATCH updates against many distinct better-auth SCIM Users resources (/scim/v2/Users/:id). On affected @better-auth/scim, a colliding-provider-ID token can resolve SSO/OIDC-provisioned users it never provisioned and rewrite global profile fields; SCIM PUT/PATCH also changed email without the create-path uniqueness check and left emailVerified stale — enabling account takeover. A colliding token enumerating and rewriting >5 distinct user resources is the fan-out signal. Rationale: Targets the advisory's second write path — PUT/PATCH to /scim/v2/Users rewriting global email/profile fields via a colliding provider ID. dcount over distinct /Users/:id paths captures the enumerate-and-rewrite fan-out that separates one caller mutating many unowned users from a normal single-target IdP update. Threshold-based, so no Sigma emitted. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/scim/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/scim
ATT&CKT1098 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IdP bulk attribute sync (job title/department/manager) touching many users after an HR data change
  • Initial SCIM provisioning backfill writing all existing users at onboarding
  • IdP re-sync following a SCIM connector configuration change or schema update
  • IdP retry storm re-issuing PUT/PATCH after a transient failure
  • Scheduled reconciliation job that periodically re-pushes all mapped attributes
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the caller IP/csUserName and enumerate which /Users/:id resources were modified; decode the SCIM token provider ID and check whether it collides with an SSO/OIDC/OAuth/social provider namespace the caller does not own. 2) Contain: Revoke the SCIM token, restrict canGenerateToken, and for any user whose email was reassigned force emailVerified reset + password/session reset to block takeover of email-keyed login. 3) Hunt: Correlate with DELETE activity on the same endpoint, audit scimProvider rows for colliding providerId, verify no duplicate/hijacked email addresses were created, and upgrade to 1.6.22 / 1.7.0-beta.10.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "/scim/v2/Users"
| where csMethod in ("PUT", "PATCH")
| where scStatus between (200 .. 299)
| summarize WriteCount = count(),
            DistinctUserResources = dcount(csUriStem),
            Methods = make_set(csMethod),
            UserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by cIP, csUserName, sSiteName
| where DistinctUserResources > 5     // one caller rewriting >5 distinct /Users/:id resources = collision fan-out
| order by WriteCount desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Don’t swing at everything
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.

references:

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "e60ab99da105ee27ee09ea64ed8eb46d8edc92ee37f039dbc3e2bb9f587a33ba", "633bd79d1efd3730234d907a2a0d98e3e253a5f0e222e4e4bf3badb3fd6aea0a", "90b1456cdbe6bc2779ea0b4736ed9a998a71ae37390331b6ba87e389a49d3d59", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "dbd8dbecaa80795c135137d69921fdba", "770dbe473180366d7b539ff2c188e551", "c2efb2dcacba6d3ccc175b6ce1b7ed0a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-23 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

In the second quarter of 2026, the continuing effects of Microsoft’s disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing platform contributed to sustained declines in several major phishing techniques, while threat actors expanded into Teams-based social engineering and employed increasingly automated and multi-stage attack chains. The post Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound email from 9i6pokerdepot.com malware-delivery campaign sender · [LLM] Endpoint resolution/connection to ClickUp stage-2 BAT dropper subdomain · [LLM] Inbound message bundling nested .eml (voicemail lure) plus calendar invite · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Financial_report.bat hidden PowerShell pulling installer.exe from pixeldrain.com · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Inbound email from 9i6pokerdepot.com malware-delivery campaign sender AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound mail from the Q2-2026 multi-stage malware campaign's DKIM-signed sender domain 9i6pokerdepot.com / Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com. Article-specific because these are the exact sender IOCs Microsoft attributed to the nested-EML → ClickUp BAT → pixeldrain chain observed 2026-06-15. Rationale: Uses the exact table-1 IOCs (9i6pokerdepot.com sending domain and Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com sender), DKIM-signed by the operator, so a match is a direct campaign hit. Cross-checked windowsnews.ai and cybersecuritynews.com which independently attribute this sender to the same chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/a-phishing-empire-fell-and-now-the-calls-are-coming-inside-microsofts-q2-2026-security-shakeup.440163 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/email-phishing-threats-as-teams-vishing-attacks/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate business partner coincidentally registered on the same reused/parked domain (unlikely for this attacker-owned domain)
  • Internal security-team replay of the phishing sample for training, sent from a lab mailbox using the same address
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation service re-sending the captured message into a monitored mailbox
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all EmailEvents rows for SenderFromDomain 9i6pokerdepot.com; confirm DeliveryAction (Delivered vs Blocked) and enumerate recipients + any UrlClickEvents on the embedded voicemail link. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message org-wide via Explorer, add sender domain + Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com to the tenant block list, and reset/quarantine any recipient who clicked. 3) Hunt: for each recipient device pivot to UC2/UC3 (t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com resolution and pixeldrain.com PowerShell download) to determine if the chain executed.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com"
    or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com"
    or SenderFromAddress =~ "Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AttachmentCount, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc

    or SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com"

Endpoint resolution/connection to ClickUp stage-2 BAT dropper subdomain AIDelivery High
Hunts DNS/HTTP for t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com, the specific ClickUp attachment subdomain hosting the stage-2 Financial_report.bat dropper in the June 2026 campaign. Distinct from the email UC — this catches execution of the lure link on the endpoint even if the mail was missed. Rationale: The full-URL IOC in table-1 row 5 pins the exact subdomain t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com; general clickup-attachments.com is a legitimate host, so matching only this operator subdomain keeps FPs near zero. Corroborated by the windowsnews.ai and cybersecuritynews.com write-ups describing the ClickUp-hosted BAT. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/a-phishing-empire-fell-and-now-the-calls-are-coming-inside-microsofts-q2-2026-security-shakeup.440163
ATT&CKT1102 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or sandbox intentionally detonating the sample and resolving the subdomain
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling pre-resolving IOCs from a feed on an analyst workstation
  • Web proxy/DNS-filter appliance performing a category lookup of the subdomain (log source is the appliance, not a real user host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the DeviceName/user that resolved the subdomain and the InitiatingProcessFileName (expect a browser or outlook.exe following the login.microsoftonline.com redirect); confirm whether a .bat was written to disk shortly after. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block clickup-attachments.com subdomain at proxy/DNS for this operator prefix, and kill/quarantine any Financial_report.bat. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 on the same host for the pixeldrain.com PowerShell download and installer.exe in %TEMP%, and sweep DeviceNetworkEvents org-wide for any other host that resolved the subdomain.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Financial_report.bat hidden PowerShell pulling installer.exe from pixeldrain.com AIInstallation High
Hunts the stage-2 execution: a BAT/cmd or hidden PowerShell whose command line references pixeldrain.com or Financial_report.bat, matching the campaign's dropper that fetched installer.exe from pixeldrain.com into %TEMP%, ran it silently, then self-deleted. Highest-fidelity endpoint pivot in the chain. Rationale: pixeldrain.com is the named final-payload host (table-1 row 6, hxxps://pixeldrain.com/api/file/3v92oJiL) and Financial_report.bat is the corroborated stage-2 filename; either string in a command line is near-unambiguous. The HiddenWindow projection and %TEMP% context match the reported '-w hidden PowerShell → installer.exe in Temp → self-delete' behaviour from the windowsnews.ai analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/a-phishing-empire-fell-and-now-the-calls-are-coming-inside-microsofts-q2-2026-security-shakeup.440163 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/email-phishing-threats-as-teams-vishing-attacks/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1564.003 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or user legitimately downloading a file shared via pixeldrain.com with curl/PowerShell (rare in enterprises but possible)
  • Security analyst manually re-running the dropper command in a sandbox for analysis
  • Red-team engagement replicating this exact chain — validate against engagement calendar before escalating
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged DeviceName inspect the full process tree — expect cmd.exe running Financial_report.bat → hidden powershell.exe with pixeldrain.com → installer.exe in %TEMP%; capture SHA256 of installer.exe before self-delete removes it. 2) Contain: isolate the device, block pixeldrain.com egress, and submit installer.exe hash to Defender for block/hunt. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for installer.exe under \Users\*\AppData\Local\Temp and DeviceNetworkEvents for pixeldrain.com across the fleet; correlate back to UC1 sender to scope all recipients.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "pixeldrain.com"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "Financial_report.bat"
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Financial_report.bat"
| extend HiddenWindow = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-w hidden","-windowstyle hidden","WindowStyle Hidden")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, HiddenWindow, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "pixeldrain.com" or CommandLine has "Financial_report.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Inbound message bundling nested .eml (voicemail lure) plus calendar invite AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the campaign's distinctive delivery envelope: a single inbound message carrying both a nested .eml attachment (disguised as a Teams voicemail) and a calendar (.ics) invite. Behavioral pivot that survives sender-domain rotation, unlike the hard IOC UCs. Rationale: The article and corroborating write-ups describe the lure as a nested .eml posing as a Teams voicemail delivered alongside a calendar invite; requiring BOTH attachment types in one inbound message is far rarer than either alone, giving a behavioral catch that outlives the 9i6pokerdepot.com domain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://windowsnews.ai/article/a-phishing-empire-fell-and-now-the-calls-are-coming-inside-microsofts-q2-2026-security-shakeup.440163
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user forwarding an email as a .eml attachment while also attaching a meeting .ics (legitimate scheduling workflow)
  • Automated ticketing/CRM systems that attach both an original-message .eml and a follow-up calendar hold
  • Executive-assistant mail that packages a forwarded thread plus an invite for the same meeting
  • Newsletter/webinar platforms sending an .ics with a forwarded confirmation message
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !endswith "yourcorp.com" and DeliveryAction != "Blocked"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the SenderFromDomain and Subject of matched messages; open the nested .eml metadata and any 'Listen to Voicemail'/login.microsoftonline.com redirect URL to judge maliciousness. 2) Contain: if the .eml link routes to a ClickUp attachment or pixeldrain payload, purge org-wide and block the sender; otherwise dismiss. 3) Hunt: for recipients who opened the message, pivot to UC2/UC3 (clickup-attachments subdomain resolution, pixeldrain.com PowerShell) to confirm no code execution followed.
let AttachAgg = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | extend Ext = tolower(tostring(FileName))
    | summarize HasEml = countif(Ext endswith ".eml" or tolower(FileType) == "eml"),
                HasIcs = countif(Ext endswith ".ics" or tolower(FileType) == "ics"),
                Files = make_set(FileName)
              by NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress
    | where HasEml > 0 and HasIcs > 0;
AttachAgg
| join kind=inner (EmailEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" | project NetworkMessageId, Timestamp, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, DeliveryAction) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Files, DeliveryAction
| order by Timestamp desc

let AttachAgg = EmailAttachmentInfo

              by NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress
    | where HasEml > 0 and HasIcs > 0;

| join kind=inner (EmailEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" | project NetworkMessageId, TimeGenerated, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, DeliveryAction) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Files, DeliveryAction

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Auth.js server-configuration error reaching production (fail-open precondition) AIExploitation High
Hunts application/stdout logs for the specific Auth.js v5 configuration-error strings that flip the `auth()` object from null to a truthy error object, causing `!!auth` checks to fail open for every request. The article itself recommends treating any `[auth][error]` line as a failed health check, so this is the root-cause detection. Rationale: Uses the exact Auth.js error identifiers named in the advisory (`[auth][error]`, `InvalidEndpoints`, `MissingSecret`) plus the user-facing server-config error string; all four confirmed as real Auth.js error classes via authjs.dev/reference/core/errors and upstream issue #11934. These strings only emit when the config is broken, i.e. exactly when the fail-open condition is active. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nextauthjs/next-auth/issues/11934 • https://authjs.dev/reference/core/errors • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-8FPG-XM3F-6CX3
ATT&CKT1556
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev/staging/preview deployments intentionally running with incomplete provider config emit [auth][error] routinely
  • CI builds surfacing MissingSecret during Next.js build since 5.0.0-beta.16 (upstream issue #10538)
  • A newly added OAuth provider misconfigured on a non-production branch preview
  • Log aggregation of test/debug output that quotes the error string verbatim
  • Deliberate DR/chaos testing of auth failure modes
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "dev" and Computer !has "staging" and Computer !has "preview" and Computer !has "-ci"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the emitting host is production (not dev/preview). If prod, the app is currently fail-open — every visitor is treated as authenticated. Check the timestamp: has this host served traffic since the first error line? 2) CONTAIN: Roll back the offending deploy or restore the missing env var (AUTH_SECRET / provider issuer). If rollback is slow, take the affected instance out of the load balancer. 3) HUNT: Pull all successful requests to protected routes on that host since FirstSeen (see the fail-open exploitation UC) to scope who accessed what while auth was broken; review for sensitive-data or privileged-action access.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
    or SyslogMessage has "InvalidEndpoints"
    or SyslogMessage has "MissingSecret"
    or SyslogMessage has "There was a problem with the server configuration"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), SampleMessage=any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Auth.js Server-Configuration Error Reaching Production (Fail-Open Precondition)
id: b3f1c2a4-7d9e-4a1b-8c2d-1f4e6a9b0c31
description: Detects Auth.js (next-auth v5) server-configuration error strings in application logs. These errors populate the auth() object with a truthy error, causing existence-based auth checks (!!auth) to fail open (GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3
  - https://authjs.dev/reference/core/errors
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/27
tags:
  - attack.t1556
  - attack.defense_evasion
logsource:
  category: application
  product: nodejs
detection:
  selection:
    message|contains:
      - '[auth][error]'
      - 'InvalidEndpoints'
      - 'MissingSecret'
      - 'There was a problem with the server configuration'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:nodejs ("[auth][error]" OR InvalidEndpoints OR MissingSecret OR "There was a problem with the server configuration")
# log group: /aws/lambda/*  (Next.js SSR / API-route function stdout)
fields @timestamp, @logStream, @message
| filter @message like /\[auth\]\[error\]/ or @message like /InvalidEndpoints/ or @message like /MissingSecret/ or @message like /There was a problem with the server configuration/
| sort @timestamp desc
CLOUD
index=* ("[auth][error]" OR "InvalidEndpoints" OR "MissingSecret" OR "There was a problem with the server configuration")
| stats earliest(_time) as firstSeen latest(_time) as lastSeen count values(source) as sources by host
| convert ctime(firstSeen) ctime(lastSeen)
| sort - lastSeen
Auth.js fail-open exploited: protected routes served 200/302 during an active auth-error window AIExploitation Medium
Correlates Auth.js `[auth][error]` log lines with successful (200/302) HTTP responses on the same host inside a short window — the observable signature of the app granting access while the auth layer is broken. This catches the vulnerability being exploited (unauthenticated visitors served protected content), not just the misconfiguration. Rationale: Ties the article's exact fail-open string (`[auth][error]`) to served-content status codes (200/302) on the same host within 10 minutes — the mechanism the advisory describes (`!!auth` true for every request while broken). Correlation on host + time isolates the exploitation from the mere presence of the error. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nextauthjs/next-auth/issues/11934 • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-8FPG-XM3F-6CX3
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately authenticated users receiving 200/302 during the same window as a transient auth error
  • Uptime/health-check probes hitting genuinely public routes returning 200
  • Static asset requests (js/css/img) returning 200 unrelated to auth-gated routes
  • A single transient OAuth provider timeout logged as [auth][error] while auth otherwise functions normally
Suppression filter
| where csUriStem !endswith ".js" and csUriStem !endswith ".css" and csUriStem !endswith ".ico" and csUriStem !endswith ".png" and csUriStem !endswith ".svg" and csUriStem !endswith ".woff2"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the 200/302 responses are to auth-protected routes (not public pages or static assets). Correlate cIP against known-authenticated sessions — unrecognised IPs receiving protected content during the error window are the strongest signal. 2) CONTAIN: If protected content was served to unauthenticated callers, roll back/fix the config (restore AUTH_SECRET or provider issuer) and pull the host from rotation; invalidate any sessions issued during the window. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every distinct src IP served 200 during all error windows on this host; check downstream logs for data export, privileged mutations, or account-takeover actions performed under the fail-open.
let ErrWindow = 10m;
let AuthErrors = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
    | project ErrTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, AuthError = SyslogMessage;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where scStatus in (200, 302)
| where csMethod in ("GET","POST")
| join kind=inner AuthErrors on Computer
| where TimeGenerated between (ErrTime .. ErrTime + ErrWindow)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, ErrTime, AuthError
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats count, values(Web.uri_path) as uri_paths, values(Web.src) as src_ips from datamodel=Web where (Web.status=200 OR Web.status=302) by Web.dest, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| join type=inner dest [ search index=* ("[auth][error]" OR "MissingSecret" OR "InvalidEndpoints") | stats count by host | rename host as dest | fields dest ]
| sort - _time
summariesonly=false

Auth.js config break on deploy: first-ever [auth][error] on a previously-healthy host AIExploitation High
Baseline anti-join that surfaces the exact moment a previously-working deployment becomes misconfigured — the article's named trigger ('an environment variable is changed or removed during a deploy'). Flags hosts emitting `[auth][error]` for the first time versus a 14-day baseline, catching the silent transition from fail-closed to fail-open. Rationale: Directly targets the advisory's stated risk narrative — a deploy removing/altering an env var flips a healthy app to fail-open. The 14-day baseline anti-join on `[auth][error]` isolates the first-time-broken transition, which is far higher-fidelity for prod than any-occurrence matching (dev noise typically pre-exists in the baseline). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8fpg-xm3f-6cx3 • https://github.com/nextauthjs/next-auth/issues/11934
ATT&CKT1556
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • First deployment of a brand-new app/host with no prior baseline (expected initial errors)
  • Host re-imaged or renamed so it appears 'new' though auth was already broken
  • Blue/green or autoscale instance coming online mid-rollout with a transient config gap
  • Baseline window shorter than an intermittent provider's error cadence, so a rare blip reads as first-seen
Suppression filter
| where Computer !has "dev" and Computer !has "staging" and Computer !has "preview" and Computer !has "-ci"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm this host had a healthy 14-day baseline and just started erroring — check whether a deploy/config change landed immediately before FirstSeen (CI/CD timeline, env-var change history). 2) CONTAIN: Treat as an active fail-open on a production host: roll back the deploy or restore the missing config value, and remove the instance from the load balancer until auth() returns null-on-failure again. 3) HUNT: Pivot to the fail-open exploitation UC for this host/window to enumerate what was accessed unauthenticated between FirstSeen and remediation; verify no privileged actions or data reads occurred.
let Baseline = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. ago(1d))
    | where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
    | summarize by Computer;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "[auth][error]"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on Computer
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), SampleMessage=any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc
APPLICATION
index=* "[auth][error]" earliest=-1d
| stats min(_time) as firstSeen count values(source) as sources by host
| where firstSeen >= relative_time(now(), "-1d")
| join type=leftanti host [ search index=* "[auth][error]" earliest=-14d latest=-1d | stats count by host | fields host ]
| convert ctime(firstSeen)
| sort - firstSeen

| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and the initiating process (browser vs. service); confirm the user has an active Zimbra webmail session and whether the org runs unpatched ZCS (<10.0.18 / <10.1.13). 2) Contain: block all nine domains/IPs at proxy+DNS, isolate the host, and force-reset the affected user's Zimbra password and 2FA scratch codes (the payload steals both). 3) Hunt: pivot on the user/device for the last 90 days of mailbox access, search all endpoints for any of the nine IOCs, and review Zimbra logs for the CSS @import XSS mail that triggered it.

Inbound HTML-attachment lure exploiting Zimbra XSS (CVE-2025-66376) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails delivered with an HTML/HTM attachment (or news-headline lure body) to webmail users — the CL-STA-1114 delivery vector that carries the obfuscated Base64/SVG payload abusing Zimbra's CSS @import XSS. Article-specific in that it targets the zero-click HTML-borne exploit rather than generic malicious attachments. Rationale: Article states initial access is a phishing email with an HTML attachment or embedded HTML carrying the Base64/SVG payload; corroborating CISA/SentinelOne detail confirms CVE-2025-66376 fires on viewing crafted HTML mail, so inbound HTML attachments to webmail users are the delivery pivot. Kept as hunting given benign HTML attachments are common. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-66376/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1203
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing/newsletter platforms that send rich HTML as an attachment
  • Automated report/invoice systems delivering .htm exports
  • Internal ticketing or monitoring tools emailing HTML dashboards inbound via a relay
  • Recruiter/CV emails with HTML resumes
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("news.example-vendor.com") and not (SenderMailFromDomain endswith "mailchimpapp.net")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the HTML attachment in a sandbox and grep for CSS @import, invisible <svg onload>, atob()/Base64 blobs, or references to the nine campaign domains. 2) Contain: if malicious, purge the message tenant-wide (soft-delete), block sender + any embedded domain, and reset the recipient's Zimbra credentials and 2FA scratch codes. 3) Hunt: confirm whether the org runs unpatched ZCS, and correlate the recipient against the C2-contact detection to see if exfiltration already occurred.
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileType in~ ("html","htm")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileType, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, ThreatTypes
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileType in~ ("html","htm")
| join kind=inner (
    EmailEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
    | where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileType, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, ThreatTypes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Browser-initiated webmail data exfiltration to CL-STA-1114 C2 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a browser process (the authenticated Zimbra session) making outbound HTTP connections to the campaign's C2 domains/IPs — the moment the injected JavaScript ships stolen credentials, 2FA scratch codes, CSRF tokens and mail archive off-box. Distinct from the broad C2 detection by requiring a browser initiator and HTTP egress shape. Rationale: Combines the campaign's confirmed C2 IOC set with a browser-process initiator, because the CVE-2025-66376 XSS runs inside the authenticated Zimbra browser session and the injected JS exfiltrates over HTTP — a browser hitting these specific hosts is high-fidelity exfil, not generic web traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa26-204a • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/russian-espionage-group-exploited.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1539 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst manually browsing to a seized/sinkholed C2 domain during investigation
  • Browser prefetch/DNS-preconnect to a domain reclaimed post-takedown
  • URL-reputation browser extension pinging a look-alike domain
  • Sandbox/detonation VM using a real browser to detonate the sample
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--headless" and DeviceName !in~ ("SANDBOX-DETONATE01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the browser had an active Zimbra session and inspect the request (POST body size, user-agent) for outbound credential/mail data. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the C2 at proxy+DNS, and immediately reset the user's Zimbra password, 2FA scratch codes, and invalidate active sessions/CSRF tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep all browsers org-wide for the nine IOCs, review the mailbox for 90-day access anomalies, and check whether the org's ZCS is unpatched.

Unpatched Zimbra Collaboration exposed to CVE-2025-66376 (Void Blizzard target) AIExploitation High
Surfaces endpoints/servers running Zimbra Collaboration versions vulnerable to CVE-2025-66376 — the CSS @import stored-XSS that CL-STA-1114 exploits zero-click. Directly supports the article's proactive-patching guidance by listing exploitable ZCS instances (10.0<10.0.18, 10.1<10.1.13). Rationale: Uses the concrete CVE-2025-66376 identifier confirmed by SentinelOne's vuln database and the CISA advisory (affected 10.0<10.0.18 / 10.1<10.1.13); a TVM exposure hunt is the cleanest way to operationalize the article's patch-now message. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2025-66376/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-exploit-zimbra-zero-click-flaw-for-email-theft/
ATT&CKT1203 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ZCS host already patched to 10.0.18/10.1.13 but TVM inventory lagging a scan cycle
  • Non-production/staging Zimbra instance not internet-exposed
  • Defender TVM mis-parsing a Zimbra build string on a Linux appliance
  • Decommissioned server still present in the device inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Zimbra build and whether the Classic Web Client (the vulnerable UI) is enabled and internet-reachable. 2) Contain: schedule emergency patch to 10.0.18 / 10.1.13, or disable the Classic UI / apply the vendor mitigation in the interim. 3) Hunt: on each exposed host, correlate against the C2-contact and browser-exfil detections and review Zimbra mail logs for crafted HTML messages abusing CSS @import.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-66376")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-66376")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel

Cisco Talos
2026-07-23 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Chaos ransomware group uses new malware "msaRAT" that hijacks browsers. The malware doesn't communicate directly with C2 but connects through the browser. It enables arbitrary command execution while hiding the attacker's IP from victims via WebRTC over TURN.

ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1486
Domainsis-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev
IPs172.86.126.18
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
